episodes.212630: Multiple thunderstorm cells were observed training across the Flat Rock Community, located just northeast of the town of Mt Airy in Surry County. Cells began crossing the area at around 5:45 pm EDT, and continued passing across the area repeatedly until around 8:15 pm EDT before rainfall became light in intensity. Rainfall rates rose to as high as 5 inches per hour multiple times through the event. Despite dry antecedent conditions with D2: Severe Drought highlighted for the northern half of Surry County by the U.S. Drought Monitor, MRMS FLASH data estimated the rainfall reached the 142-year Average Recurrence Interval ceiling for a 3-hour duration in the Flat Rock area, with rainfall totals reaching 120 percent of the 3-hour Flash Flood Guidance. CREST Unit Streamflow was unimpressive however, reaching into the 300 to 400 cfs per mi^2 by around 8:00 pm EDT. The heavy rain produced runoff around 6 inches deep across Highway 103 from a nearby hillside drainage.

Environmental analysis during the late afternoon hours across central Pennsylvania exhibited ample instability (with SBCAPE values exceeding 3000 J/kg across the entire region), steep low-level lapse rates, and ample DCAPE values exceeding 1000 J/kg. While shear was not the most sufficient, ample instability allowed for storms to continue in a broken line as they shifted eastward across the region through the evening hours. Widespread wind damage was reported along the broken line of thunderstorms, with numerous trees down across much of the forecast area south of the Interstate 80 corridor. Across areas north of the Interstate 80 corridor, scattered instances of wind damage were reported, with the most widespread in Lycoming County.

In addition, sharp rises on area creeks and streams led to overland flooding in a few spots...most notably on the north side of Lexington in McLean County.  The flood waters gradually receded after sunrise on June 11th.
episodes.214146: On June 10th, daytime heating pushed temperatures into the upper 80s and lower 90s, combining with surging humidity to drive heat indices near 100��F and create a highly unstable environment with MLCAPE values reaching 2,500 J/kg. Weak low-level convergence initially triggered severe storms over Wayne County, which dropped 1 to 1.25-inch hail across Dearborn and Dearborn Heights. Later in the evening, a destructive Midwestern squall line tracked into southern Lower Michigan, though it steadily weakened as it moved through Southeast Michigan before completely clearing the state by midnight. While the broader system left over 85,000 customers without power statewide, wind damage, downed trees, and power outages within Southeast Michigan remained isolated to scattered, impacting communities primarily along and west of U.S. 23.
episodes.214156: A strong storm system interacted with a highly unstable and sheared environment to produce a significant severe weather outbreak across central Illinois during the late afternoon and evening of June 11th.  Scattered supercell thunderstorms initially developed west of the I-55 corridor along a pre-frontal trough during the afternoon.  One of these storms produced an EF-3 tornado that impacted portions of Woodford and Marshall counties and dropped tennis ball-sized hail (2.50 diameter).  Additional cells rapidly developed further west across southeastern Iowa into northern Missouri ahead of an advancing cold front.  These storms congealed into a line and pushed eastward into central Illinois during the evening.  Widespread damaging wind gusts of 60-70mph occurred with the line along and north of the I-72 corridor.  After storm surveys were completed, it was discovered an additional 8 tornadoes were embedded within the line...creating pockets of enhanced damage.

episodes.214502: On June 11, 2026, a severe flash flood event impacted Carroll County, New Hampshire, devastating numerous roads in the town of Madison and surrounding areas. The event was driven by a slow-moving warm front interacting with an unstable and moist airmass. This setup allowed a cluster of deep convection to train continuously over the region, producing extreme localized rainfall rates that peaked at an estimated 4 inches per hour. Total accumulations reached 5.47 inches near Albany and a public report of 4.45 inches in Madison, qualifying the deluge as a 100-year average recurrence interval (ARI) event. The extreme flooding was heavily exacerbated by saturated antecedent soil conditions left behind by a remarkably wet May, which had already seen double its typical rainfall.

A tornado with estimated peak winds of 110 mph touched down near Sandy Creek, southwest of the intersection of N 8th Road and E 8th Road. The tornado moved northeast through fields and crossed E 9th Road. The tornado crossed Route 17 where it snapped large tree limbs off the top of a tree and blew down a utility pole. Windows were also blown out of a nearby house. The tornado destroyed multiple machine sheds in the 900 block of Route 17 with debris strewn almost a mile downstream. Storm chaser video showed at least three fast moving sub-vortices as the tornado continued northeast crossing E 10th Road. The tornado then reached its maximum width of nearly 500 yards with significant cycloidal markings in a field east of E 10th Road. The tornado continued moving northeast until it ended in a field south of N 10th Road. High resolution satellite imagery was used to determine most of the path of this tornado.

A tornado with estimated peak winds of 105 mph touched down along County Road E 2200 North, west of Route 23. The tornado may not have been fully condensed to the ground or consisted of intermittent touchdowns along the first two thirds of the path where only minor tree damage was noted. A photo from a storm chaser showed a couple of mesovortices crossing Interstate 55. Minor tree damage continued as the tornado moved through Odell and areas west of Route 47. Based on storm chaser videos, the tornado appeared to rapidly strengthen and widen while crossing Route 47. Sporadic tree damage continued along the path until utility poles were broken and leaning along E 3000 North Road and N 3100 East Road. Drone imagery showed swirl marks in fields west of N 3200 East Road. Several outbuildings and a garage were destroyed just east of N 3200 East Road and a house had a significant portion of its roof structure removed. Several farm buildings and a garage were destroyed just east of N 3300 East Road, south of Route 17. A large barn was tipped on its side. Significant tree damage also occurred. The porch roof on a house collapsed along Route 17 in Blair. A wall of a farm building was removed with debris blown into a field. The tornado continued northeast and ended in a field near railroad tracks, just south of the Livingston LaSalle County line.

A tornado which touched down near Long Point in Livingston County, moved northeast and crossed into LaSalle County just east of Prairie Grove Road and was likely at peak intensity as it crossed into LaSalle County as well as at its maximum width of 600 yards. The tornado heavily damaged several houses along E 12th Street and Sunbury Drive. Only the inner-most walls of a one-story house on E 12th Street remained standing. Two people in the house were both injured, a woman who suffered lacerations across her body and a man who suffered leg or ankle injuries and was rescued by police officers. A total of 7 people were injured in this area, 4 of whom were transported to a local hospital. The tornado crossed Route 18 and moved generally north along Airport Road. Just north of Route 18, a garage and a farm outbuilding were destroyed and a house suffered minor roof damage. South of N 14th Road a split-level house lost a good portion of its exterior walls and its entire roof. A detached garage was destroyed. Numerous utility poles were blown down along E 1st Street. The tornado continued northeast until it ended in a field north of N 1475th Road.
